policy_title: Achieve a zero-carbon economy through energy transition and green investment
stated: Transition to a zero-carbon society more than a decade ahead of 2050, by ending all new fossil fuel extraction projects and cancelling recent licences like Rosebank, and ending all subsidies to the oil and gas industries. This includes accelerating wind energy development to provide around 70% of UK electricity by 2030, with targets of 80GW offshore, 53GW onshore, and 100GW solar by 2035, and ending the de-facto ban on onshore wind. The plan involves expanding community and public ownership of energy infrastructure, removing regulatory barriers, investing in community energy via regional banks, and bringing the Crown Estate into public ownership. A just transition will be supported with £4bn per year investment in skills and training for workers in carbon-intensive industries to transition to green jobs, and the establishment of an Offshore Energy and Skills Passport. The electricity grid will be significantly expanded and improved, with increased capacity for energy storage and closer connection with Europe. The policy also calls for ceasing development of new nuclear power stations due to high costs and phasing out existing ones. Overall, an average of £40bn per year will be invested over the next parliament in a green economic transformation, including £7bn annually on climate adaptation, involving public and private sector participation. Financial services will be required to divest from fossil fuel assets by 2030, and the Bank of England's mandate will include funding sustainability. Regional mutual banks will be set up with £10bn public money to invest in SMEs and community-owned enterprises for decarbonisation, supplemented by £2bn per year in grants for businesses from local authorities. Investment in R&D will increase by over £30bn across five years, focusing on climate and environmental solutions like energy storage, agroecological agriculture, and carbon-neutral construction.

source.quote: Green MPs will push the next government to stop all new fossil fuel extraction projects in the United Kingdom and to cancel recently issued fossil fuel licences, such as for Rosebank. We will also end all subsidies to the oil and gas industries. The UK’s current climate targets do not reflect the urgency of the climate crisis or what is required by global justice. We would push the government to transition to a zero-carbon society as soon as possible, and more than a decade ahead of 2050. Green MPs will aim to introduce new support and incentives to directly accelerate wind energy development...This will pave the way for wind to provide around 70% of the UK’s electricity by 2030. Our targets are to achieve 80GW of offshore wind, 53 GW of onshore wind, and 100 GW of solar by 2035. We will end the de-facto ban on onshore wind. We are committed to the energy sector being under local democratic control as far as is possible. We will push for: • A minimum threshold of community ownership in all sustainable energy infrastructure. • The removal of regulatory barriers to community energy. • Investment in community energy by regional investment banks. The Crown Estate will be brought into public ownership and should open more coastal waters for offshore wind and marine energy. Control over its assets within the jurisdiction of Wales should be devolved to the Welsh Government, as it is in Scotland. There needs to be a just transition, led by workers and unions, that sees communities reap the rewards of the shift to green energy. As part of this, we will push the next government to establish an Offshore Energy and Skills Passport so that workers can transition more easily between offshore energy industries. Elected Greens will push for: • Investment in skills and training (including retrofitting) reaching £4bn per year, allowing workers to be prepared for the transition and the new roles they can take on. Elected Greens will seek to significantly expand and improve the efficiency of the electricity grid, increasing its capacity so that it can distribute the increased electricity the UK will need as it transitions away from fossil fuels. We would connect our electricity supply more closely to that of our neighbours in Europe to provide a broader-based supply we can call on when needed and to allow us to export electricity when we have a surplus. We would rapidly expand the capacity for energy storage, so that there is security of electricity supply for short-term peaks in demand and periods of low supply from variable renewables. We would cease development of new nuclear power stations, as nuclear energy is much more expensive and slower to develop than renewables. Green MPs will campaign to phase out existing nuclear power stations. Elected Greens would push for significant investment in a green economic transformation, alongside the private sector. This programme to include: • An average of £40bn per year over the course of the next parliament, including £7bn annually on climate adaptation. Any company holding a UK banking licence will be required to present an investment strategy outlining a clear pathway to divestment of its current fossil fuel assets as soon as possible, and at least by 2030. The Bank of England’s mandate will be changed so that funding the sustainability transition becomes a central objective, alongside the maintenance of price stability. Non-bank financial institutions, such as UK pension funds, investment funds, mutual funds, brokers and insurance companies that sell policies in the UK, will need to remove fossil fuel assets from their investment portfolios, securities transactions and balance sheets by 2030. Green MPs will back the setting up of regional mutual banks to drive investment in decarbonisation and local economic sustainability by supporting investment in SMEs and community-owned enterprises and cooperatives. These banks will be capitalised through a Cooperative Development Fund using some of the funds made available through the United Kingdom Infrastructure Bank (UKIB), along with an additional £10bn of public money. We will give local authorities £2bn per year to provide grants to help businesses decarbonise. We will explore legal ways for companies to be transformed into mutual organisations, especially at the point of succession from one owner to another. Green MPs will seek to increase investment into research and development by over £30bn in the lifetime of the five-year parliament. Additional spending will be primarily focused on tackling the climate and environmental crisis through funding research into sectors including: energy storage; agroecological agriculture and soil health; re-use, repair, recycling and designing out waste; carbon neutral construction; carbon-neutral production and carbon capture technology.

bearing_set.reason: The policy's entire stated purpose is eliminating carbon emissions via renewable build-out, ending fossil fuel extraction, and £40bn/year green investment — directly and substantially affecting the UK's emissions trajectory and air/water quality indicators.

Energy bills are a core O2 indicator; the transition from fossil fuels to renewables changes household energy costs both near-term (transition costs, possible price volatility from ending gas extraction) and long-term (lower marginal-cost generation), producing a non-negligible and contested verdict on affordability.

The explicit £4bn/year just-transition package for retraining workers in carbon-intensive industries, the Offshore Energy and Skills Passport, and the green-job creation from £40bn/year investment directly affect employment, job security, and pay for a significant cohort of workers.

£40bn/year green investment, £30bn+ R&D over five years, grid infrastructure and storage, and a regional banking system are designed to shift the UK's productive base — a real dual-horizon effect on aggregate living standards and productivity.

A £40bn/year public investment commitment at this scale is non-negligible for debt-path sustainability; whether it is funded or borrowed, and whether it constitutes productive investment or consumption, determines the intergenerational balance-sheet effect.

Community and public ownership of energy infrastructure, £10bn regional mutual banks, and per-business grants explicitly target who captures the economic rents from green energy — a concrete distributional mechanism affecting the rich-poor gap and regional inequality.

A domestic renewable buildout replacing imported fossil fuels directly affects energy-supply resilience to external threats — an O5 national-security indicator that became material post-Ukraine and is moved concretely by this policy's extraction ban and grid-independence goals.

membership_note: This is a comprehensive, multi-sector industrial-transformation policy; 7 bearings are justified by its explicit mechanisms across energy costs, public investment, labour markets, distributional ownership structures, and national energy security — not by generous reading but by named indicators each bearing earns.
